title: Building a Raycast Extension with React
summary: Build a Raycast extension with React and TypeScript: create a live npm package search with List, keyboard actions, user preferences, and Store publishing.
body_markdown:
A Raycast extension is an npm project written in React and TypeScript. Your components return Raycast primitives such as` List` ,` Detail` and` ActionPanel` , and Raycast draws them in its own interface, so you never write HTML, DOM code or CSS.


Most developers have a few lookups they run dozens of times a day, like finding a package name, checking its version and copying the install line. Those small trips through a browser tab add up. This guide builds one complete command, a live npm package search, with a List view, keyboard actions, a user preference, and the steps to publish it to the Store.


## Key Takeaways


- Each entry in the` commands` array of` package.json` maps to a file in` src/` with the same name, and the default-exported React component in that file runs when the command opens.
- ` useFetch` from` @raycast/utils` returns` data` and` isLoading` , and its` execute` option delays the request until the query is ready.
- Setting` throttle` on` List` delays` onSearchTextChange` while the user types, which suits search that hits the network.
- ` npm run publish` opens a pull request against` raycast/extensions` , and Raycast publishes the extension to the Store once that PR is reviewed and merged.


## What Is a Raycast Extension?


A Raycast extension adds commands to the search bar of Raycast, a keyboard-driven launcher for macOS and Windows. As the[Raycast for Windows announcement](https://www.raycast.com/blog/raycast-for-windows) puts it, extensions are built with React and TypeScript. So if you know web development, you already know how to build for Raycast. The main difference is the render target. You don’t write markup. You compose Raycast’s components, and Raycast draws them with its own native-looking styling. The same idea shows up in OpenReplay’s article on[building command-line apps with React Ink](https://blog.openreplay.com/building-command-line-apps-with-react-ink/) , where React renders to a terminal instead of the DOM.


## How Do You Create a Raycast Extension?


To create a Raycast extension, open Raycast, run the **Create Extension** command (it requires sign-in), pick a List-based template, and choose a folder. Then install and start the dev server:


```text
npm   install   &&   npm   run   dev
```


The[Getting Started page](https://developers.raycast.com/basics/getting-started) asks for npm 7 or higher and Node.js 22.14 or higher, but the[API changelog](https://developers.raycast.com/misc/changelog) entry for version 2.0.0 (August 25, 2026) raises the CLI’s minimum to Node.js 22.22.2, so install that version or newer. As the[Create Your First Extension](https://developers.raycast.com/basics/create-your-first-extension) guide describes,` npm run dev` puts the command at the top of root search with hot reloading. The command stays installed after you stop the dev server. The entry file is` ./src/index.tsx` .


## Project Layout and the package.json Manifest


The` package.json` file is both your npm config and the extension manifest. Raycast reads commands, metadata and preferences from it. The[manifest reference](https://developers.raycast.com/information/manifest) defines these fields:


Field Purpose


` name` Unique extension identifier


` title` Display name in Raycast and the Store


` description` ,` icon` Store listing text and image


` author` Your Raycast Store handle


` categories` Store categories; at least one is required to publish


` commands\[\].name` Command ID; matches` src/<name>.tsx`


` commands\[\].mode`` view` for commands that render UI


` preferences\[\]` User settings shown in Raycast


` platforms`` "macOS"` and/or` "Windows"`


```text
{
"  $schema  "  :   "  https://www.raycast.com/schemas/extension.json  "  ,
"  name  "  :   "  npm-search  "  ,
"  title  "  :   "  npm Search  "  ,
"  description  "  :   "  Search the npm registry from Raycast  "  ,
"  icon  "  :   "  extension-icon.png  "  ,
"  author  "  :   "  your-raycast-username  "  ,
"  license  "  :   "  MIT  "  ,
"  categories  "  : [  "  Developer Tools  "  ],
"  platforms  "  : [  "  macOS  "  ,   "  Windows  "  ],
"  commands  "  : [
{   "  name  "  :   "  index  "  ,   "  title  "  :   "  Search npm Packages  "  ,   "  description  "  :   "  Search npm and open or copy results  "  ,   "  mode  "  :   "  view  "   }
],
"  preferences  "  : [
{   "  name  "  :   "  resultLimit  "  ,   "  type  "  :   "  textfield  "  ,   "  required  "  :   false  ,   "  default  "  :   "  20  "  ,   "  title  "  :   "  Result Limit  "  ,   "  description  "  :   "  Maximum packages to show  "   }
]
}
```


Keep the` dependencies` block that the template generated. Don’t copy version pins from older tutorials.


## Search npm Packages with List and useFetch


To search as the user types, pass a state setter to` List` ’s` onSearchTextChange` and feed that query into` useFetch` . According to the[List reference](https://developers.raycast.com/api-reference/user-interface/list) , adding an` onSearchTextChange` handler turns off Raycast’s built-in filtering, so the list shows the registry’s results as they arrive. The same reference suggests turning on` throttle` whenever your own search logic makes async calls, such as network requests.


The[npm registry search endpoint](https://github.com/npm/registry/blob/main/docs/REGISTRY-API.md) is` GET /-/v1/search` . It accepts` text` and` size` (default 20, max 250) and returns an` objects` array in which each entry has a` package` with` name` ,` version` ,` description` and` links.npm` .


```text
import   {   Action  ,   ActionPanel  ,   List  ,   getPreferenceValues   }   from   "  @raycast/api  "  ;
import   {   useFetch   }   from   "  @raycast/utils  "  ;
import   {   useState   }   from   "  react  "  ;


type   NpmSearch   =   {
objects  :   {   package  :   {   name  :   string  ;   version  :   string  ;   description  ?:   string  ;   links  :   {   npm  :   string   }   }   }[];
};


export default   function   Command  ()   {
const   {   resultLimit   }   =   getPreferenceValues  <{   resultLimit  ?:   string   }>();
const   size   =   Math  .  min  (  Number  (  resultLimit  )   ||   20  ,   250  );
const   [  query  ,   setQuery  ]   =   useState  (  ""  );
const   hasQuery   =   query  .  trim  ().  length   >   0  ;


const   {   data  ,   isLoading   }   =   useFetch  <  NpmSearch  >(
`  https://registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/search?text=  ${  encodeURIComponent  (  query  )  }  &size=  ${  size  }`  ,
{   execute  :   hasQuery  ,   keepPreviousData  :   true   },
);


const   packages   =   hasQuery   ?   (  data  ?.  objects   ??   [])   :   [];


return   (
<  List   isLoading  =  {isLoading}   onSearchTextChange  =  {setQuery}   throttle   searchBarPlaceholder  =  "  Search npm packages  "  >
<  List.EmptyView   title  =  {hasQuery   ?   "  No packages found  "   :   "  Type to search npm  "  } />
{packages  .  map  (({   package  :   pkg   })   =>   (
<  List.Item
key  =  {pkg  .  name}
title  =  {pkg  .  name}
subtitle  =  {pkg  .  description}
accessories  =  {  [{   text  :   pkg  .  version   }]  }
actions  =  {
<  ActionPanel  >
<  Action.OpenInBrowser   url  =  {pkg  .  links  .  npm} />
<  Action.CopyToClipboard   title  =  "  Copy Install Command  "   content  =  {  `  npm install   ${  pkg  .  name  }`  } />
</  ActionPanel  >
}
/>
))  }
</  List  >
);
}
```


The[useFetch](https://developers.raycast.com/utilities/react-hooks/usefetch)` execute` flag lets you define the hook right away but wait until all the arguments are ready before the request runs.` keepPreviousData` keeps the last results on screen while the next request is in flight, which stops the list from flickering.


In` useFetch` ,` data` stays` undefined` until the first response arrives. A call like` data.objects.map(...)` therefore throws on the first render. The` data?.objects ?? \[\]` fallback covers that render, and` isLoading` shows the spinner in the meantime.


## Add Actions: Open in Browser and Copy to Clipboard


An` ActionPanel` attached to each` List.Item` turns a result into something the user can act on. The[Actions reference](https://developers.raycast.com/api-reference/user-interface/actions) defines both components used here.` Action.OpenInBrowser` opens a URL in the default browser, then closes the main window.` Action.CopyToClipboard` copies the content, hides the main window and confirms the copy with a HUD.


Action order matters in a Raycast` ActionPanel` . According to the[Raycast manual](https://manual.raycast.com/action-panel) , pressing ↵ triggers the primary action (the first action in the list) immediately, and ⌘K opens the full panel. Put the action users want most often first.


## Read a Preference with getPreferenceValues


Settings such as result limits or API tokens belong in the manifest’s` preferences` array. The command reads them at runtime with[getPreferenceValues](https://developers.raycast.com/api-reference/preferences) . Raycast shows a settings form for every declared preference, so you don’t need to build any UI for it.


The npm search example passes an inline type argument to` getPreferenceValues` . Raycast also generates a global` Preferences` type from the manifest, so` getPreferenceValues<Preferences>()` stays in sync automatically, as code in the[raycast/extensions repository](https://github.com/raycast/extensions) commonly does. If you switch to a GitHub search, declare a` password` -type` githubToken` preference and send it as an` Authorization` header through` useFetch` ’s request options.


## How Do You Publish a Raycast Extension?


Publishing a Raycast extension means opening a pull request against the` raycast/extensions` repository. Run lint and build first:


npm script Runs Use


` dev`` ray develop` Local development with hot reload


` build`` ray build` Production build check


` lint` /` fix-lint`` ray lint` /` ray lint --fix` Fix every issue before publishing


` publish`` npx @raycast/api@latest publish` Opens the Store PR


The[Publish an Extension](https://developers.raycast.com/basics/publish-an-extension) page describes the flow.` npm run publish` asks you to authenticate with GitHub, opens the PR automatically, and squashes your commits. Raycast reviews the PR and may request changes. Once the PR is merged, the extension goes to the Store automatically.


On Windows, the[Raycast for Windows page](https://www.raycast.com/windows) says all extensions that do not require native code will work out of the box on both platforms. Set` platforms` to` \["macOS", "Windows"\]` to opt in. The[Store guidelines](https://developers.raycast.com/basics/prepare-an-extension-for-store) require` platforms` to match what the extension actually needs, so restrict it if you call platform-specific APIs.


## Conclusion


A useful Raycast extension needs three pieces: a` List` driven by throttled search, an` ActionPanel` that puts the most common action on ↵, and preferences declared in the manifest. Run` npm run dev` on the command above, swap the npm endpoint for the API you query most, and run` npm run lint` until it passes before you open your Store PR.


## FAQs


What is the difference between view, no-view and menu-bar commands in a Raycast extension?


The mode field on each commands entry decides how the command runs. A view command default-exports a React component that Raycast renders as the main UI, such as a List or Detail. A no-view command exports an async function and talks to the user through APIs like showHUD or showToast, which suits opening a URL. A menu-bar command returns a MenuBarExtra item shown in the macOS menu bar.


Can I share a Raycast extension with my team without publishing it to the public Store?


Yes. Set the owner field in package.json to your Raycast organization handle, then run npm run publish. For a private extension, the command verifies, builds and publishes it straight to the organization's private store. It opens no pull request against raycast/extensions, and only members of that organization can install it. You must be logged in, and npx ray login handles that from the CLI.


Can I style a Raycast extension with CSS or custom HTML?


No. Raycast renders its supported React components to its own native UI, so there is no stylesheet or DOM to target. You customize through component props such as icons, tag colors and list accessories. For richer content, the Detail component renders a CommonMark markdown string with an optional metadata panel, and raycast-width and raycast-height query parameters on markdown images set their size.
